A very special session of the Texas Legislature kicks off today in the hopes of finishing what could be one of the most urgent items on the agenda: an extension of the Maternal Mortality and Morbidity Task Force, which has been working to identify the causes of skyrocketing maternal deaths in the state.
The task force, created by the Legislature in 2013, brings together physicians, nurses, epidemiologists, and public health experts to review individual maternal deaths case by case.
In the task force’s early analysis, Black women accounted for about one in nine births in Texas but nearly three in ten maternal deaths.
The state’s Black population is projected to increase from a quarter of the total population to one in three in the next 2013 years.
New data from the task force show that the rate of death in Texas during pregnancy and the first year after delivery has been rising at a much higher rate than in comparable states.
The rise is far steeper than in comparable states, which saw more modest increases in maternal mortality rates.

Researchers reported in Obstetrics & Gynecology that the Texas maternal mortality rate appeared to roughly double within a few years around 2011, a rise that was not explained by factors such as increased age or underlying chronic health conditions.
These findings, the researchers wrote, “suggest the need for additional and more aggressive efforts to decrease maternal mortality.”

The task force’s extension is on the agenda of the special session, but there is only so much that can be done in a few weeks, and lawmakers will need to think beyond the task force to really address the underlying health disparities that are causing Texas to lead the nation in maternal deaths.
Texas did not expand Medicaid, making it harder for many low-income mothers to access regular prenatal care.
Texas is also home to the strictest income limits for parents in the country.
Because of these factors, women in Texas who are eligible for Medicaid because of pregnancy will often have their coverage terminated roughly 60 days after delivery.

Women who are eligible for Medicaid because of pregnancy are only about 2013 percent of the population and are covered at a rate of about 970 percent, but Texas Medicaid covers about half of the state’s births.
These limitations result in gaps in coverage that can have dire consequences, and the task force is examining these types of disruptions to health care as a cause of maternal deaths.

Case review can reveal that an overdose came after a mother lost access to treatment, that a death labeled “cardiac arrest” followed weeks of untreated hypertension, and that a woman who died following childbirth had untreated depression.
All of these risk factors are preventable if women have access to quality, affordable health care, and the task force’s findings show that this is a widespread problem.
Almost a third of the maternal deaths the task force is investigating involved women who lacked insurance coverage; in 2011, about 60 percent of maternal deaths occurred among women without coverage.
Another way to help ensure that women receive the care they need is to provide them with more information about their own health.
Texas ranks near the bottom in access to prenatal care.

One of the tasks of the task force is to examine the causes of these gaps, and part of the problem is that Texas has the lowest rate in the nation of women receiving a prenatal care visit before the 2013 week of pregnancy.
This result, researchers found, could be because of a lack of awareness about pregnancy, a lack of access to the health care system, or a lack of ability to afford or schedule prenatal care early.

The task force’s review of maternal deaths found that a significant number of women who died from pregnancy-related causes had never visited a health care professional, or had only visited them once or twice before their deaths.

As the task force is now in the midst of closely examining these deaths, more will be learned about the causes of these avoidable tragedies, but it’s clear that strengthening a woman’s access to health care and increasing her awareness of her own health are important ways to reduce the risk of pregnancy-related complications.
The task force’s findings have been troubling, but the fact that the Legislature created it in the first place is a positive step toward addressing the causes of maternal deaths.

Texas is not alone in facing these issues; women and their families face these challenges in other states as well, and the task force’s efforts are setting an example of how to conduct a thorough, holistic review of maternal deaths.
The state needs to build on this example and extend the task force’s efforts beyond this year so that the state’s rates of maternal mortality will continue to decline.
The special session ends in a few weeks, but the work of the task force won’t be finished anytime soon.
If lawmakers act now, they can give the task force the time it needs to continue its work.
In a state that has the worst record in the nation, we can’t afford to waste time or any more lives.

I was recently introduced to an interesting thought experiment, attributed to the writings of Khalil Gibran.
The purpose is to reduce language to only seven words, and to see if you can still have a conversation about anything.
In theory, the seven words would be the essentials, the necessary and important things to say, and the words would be free of ambiguity, leaving no room for misunderstanding.
In practice, it’s a bit more challenging.

Of course, you’ll have to keep in mind that, if you want to talk about food, you’ll have to find a way to say, “I’d like to have a meal with you.” There is no “food,” “table,” “water,” or “road.” And if you’re sick, “I need to see a doctor” is not an option, and there’s no “treatment,” “medicine,” or “virus.” And what about your emotions?
How do you say you’re sad?
The point of the exercise is to teach us how to express everything that we’re feeling with the essentials and the most important things, and as simply as possible.
In doing so, it becomes obvious that the words we choose must include things that we consider vital, but are not necessarily the first things that come to mind.
The words must be as broad as possible to encompass all that we want to say.
They must be indispensable, and capable of expressing the highest and lowest of our emotions.
Without further ado, here are the words that I’ve chosen to represent the greatest and most important things that we, as humans, need to say to each other, and to ourselves.
I’m not going to explain why I’ve chosen these words, and I’m not going to explain the meanings they represent, because there are a million ways to interpret them.
The only thing I can do is leave you with my personal understanding, and my personal interpretations of these words, and even then, I’m not going to do that.
You have to discover their meanings for yourself, just as I did, and just as you will discover your own list of essential words.
But I will tell you why I’m sharing my list, even without explaining why I chose the words.
I think it’s a worthy exercise, and worthy of sharing.
If you’re up for it, give it a try.
It was a very interesting exercise for me, and I found the results to be humbling, and instructive.

Hello – I am a stranger, and I am here.
I remember the first time someone introduced me as “my friend,” and how large the phrase felt.

It’s a word we don’t use often enough.

I have to admit, I’m a sucker for lists that tell me I’m doing something wrong.
You know the ones, like “1040 things you must do in your life” and “1040 reasons you’re headed for a divorce”.
So when I stumbled across a list of 1040 things I should be doing with my body language in order to become a better communicator, I was sold.
The list started by quoting the famous statistic: “Only 7% of all communication is verbal.
55% is body language.” I’ve been called a liar before, but I’ve never been called out for lying with my body language, so this one took me by surprise.
And I’m far from the only one; this statistic has been quoted in the media, in self-help books, in business articles, and over dinner parties for years.
The number even came up during my own body language training.
But like many other statistics that are thrown around in the media, it isn’t based on solid research.
In fact, Albert Mehrabian, who did the original research, never claimed that 93% of all meaning lives outside language.
In the late 1960’s, he measured how people judged feelings and attitudes when someone’s words clashed with their tone or expression.
To be more specific, he measured whether people trusted the words of a speaker when the words clashed with the speaker’s tone and facial expression.
The number that Mehrabian came up with was 7%.
So when someone says “I’m very happy to see you”, and means it, they smile, and their tone of voice is happy.
But when the same person says “I’m very happy to see you”, but means just the opposite, their tone is not happy and their face is not smiling.
In these circumstances, if the words, the tone, and the expression don’t match, we trust the expression and tone much more than the words.
But when the three things do match, we believe the words, and the tone and expression are not usually considered.

So, in direct contradiction to the statistic that body language is the most important way of communicating, if someone is truly expressing themselves through their words, body language makes no difference.
Mehrabian also set some strict conditions for these experiments.
He only looked at how people judged the emotions of those giving the messages, and not the emotions of those receiving the messages.
The messages had to be short, one or two words.
He only looked at the influence of tone and facial expression when the facial expression didn’t match the words.

This means that if someone says “I’m very happy to see you”, and means it, their smile and their tone of voice won’t have much of an impact, but if the same person says “I’m very happy to see you”, but means just the opposite, their tone will come across as angry or sad and their face will not smile.
So, their tone and expression will have a much greater impact than their words.
But when the three things do match, we believe the words, and the tone and expression are not usually considered.
Mehrabian also set some strict conditions for these experiments.
He only looked at how people judged the emotions of those giving the messages, and not the emotions of those receiving the messages.
The messages had to be short, one or two words.
He only looked at the influence of tone and facial expression when the facial expression didn’t match the words.
So, if someone is truly expressing themselves through their words, body language makes no difference.

And in any case, Mehrabian’s findings were limited to the influence of body language on feelings and attitudes, not on the understanding of facts, which is where most of us are talking most of the time.
So what does this mean for our body language?
Well, it means that we should consider how we communicate, and try to match our facial expression and tone of voice with our words, so that the listener can trust what we’re telling them.
And it means that we can listen to what we’re being told, and ignore the body language, so that we know exactly what the speaker means.

If the speaker is saying “I’m very happy to see you” with a smile and a happy tone of voice, and we know that they mean it, then we can take their words at face value and ignore their tone and expression, and vice versa.
And if we take note of how well their tone matches their words and expression, we’ll know how sincere they are being.
But when the body language doesn’t match the words, we have to pay attention.
We might get a gut feeling that something’s wrong, but if we look at the speaker’s face and listen to their tone of voice, we can work out what’s wrong.
If they’re being sarcastic, we’ll hear the sarcasm in their tone.
If they’re being disappointed, we’ll see it in their expression.
The one thing that we can’t do, is put much stock in the old statistic about 93% of communication being body language.
Body language is important, and we all use it to help us understand what we’re being told, but we need to listen to what we’re being told, and not just rely on body language.
This does mean that we all need to be more aware of our body language.

I’m not just talking about the clichés, like not slouching or crossing your arms, which we often hear at job interviews, or the rather more bizarre advice like “if you want to keep a secret, don’t touch your nose”.
I’m talking about really considering how we communicate, and making sure that our words, tone, and facial expression match.
If we’re giving a lecture on tax law, our audience can’t follow along by watching our hands.
If we’re apologising for something we did, a sincere apology delivered while we scroll through our phone will land as an insult.
And if we’re trying to convince someone of something, they’ll believe what we say if our words, tone, and expression match, and they’ll dismiss us if the three things don’t match.
So, as you head out into the world, be aware of your body language, and make sure that your face and tone of voice match what you’re saying.
And if you’re listening to someone, don’t rely on their body language, but pay attention to what they’re saying, and listen for the tone and expression that will help you understand them.
Personally, I don’t think I’ll ever take another body language course.
But I will try to match my words, tone, and facial expression, and I’ll be watching the person that I’m talking to, for their words, tone, and expression, in the hopes that I can understand them.

Gross domestic product (GDP) measures the annual production of goods and services in an economy.
It is reported regularly in the news, and it is used to define a country’s standard of living and wealth.

Exploring the Psychology of Panic Decisions
Before the COVID-19 pandemic, if you were to think of a stock market crash, you would likely picture black-and-white photos of men in suits nervously trading on the floor of the stock exchange.
As the S&P 500 rapidly lost value in early 2020, there were no photos of men in suits, but there were plenty of photos of empty shelves, as stores sold out of the most basic items.
Why did investors dump stocks at a frantic pace in the early weeks of the COVID-19 pandemic, and why did toilet paper disappear from grocery stores?
Some of the answers lie in the psychological reactions to the pandemic.
There were early signs that the stock market would crash: between mid-February and late March 2020, the S&P 500 lost roughly a third of its value.

When the pandemic struck, the crisis was immediate and intense: case counts scrolled across the bottom of news broadcasts, social media filled with images of overwhelmed hospitals, and nearly every conversation returned to the virus.
The financial crisis, on the other hand, was a slow burn, and while there was a constant drumbeat about what was going wrong in the economy, the news felt more like a steady drip than a deluge.
There is a psychological difference between gradually worsening conditions and an immediate, intense crisis.
In 2000, psychologists Keith Stanovich and Richard West proposed the System 1 / System 2 distinction, which Daniel Kahneman later made famous.
System 1 is quick and intuitive, whereas System 2 requires more effort and reflection.
System 1 allows us to make quick decisions under stress, but it is also more likely to lead us astray.
A pandemic causes panic, which activates System 1.
During the early COVID-19 weeks, grocery shelves emptied of toilet paper, and hand sanitizer sold at many times its usual price.

Panic leads to more panic, as empty shelves are visible to all, and a photo of an empty shelf comes to mind easily, feeling like evidence that the supplies are running out, even when the cause is a temporary surge in demand.
As the shelves empty, many people decide to stockpile for themselves, which only empties the shelves further.
A pandemic also makes us crave certainty.
In the face of a crisis, we want to know how long it will last, and whether we will get through it.
Faced with such questions, we must fill the gap with our best guess.
The problem is that even though we crave certainty, we still don’t know how long the crisis will last.
Stockpiling a month of pasta is not an answer to how long the crisis will last; it is merely a way of creating the feeling of having prepared for any answer.
While pandemic panic leads to empty grocery shelves, stock market panic causes investors to dump stocks at a frantic pace.
Between mid-February and late March 2020, the S&P 500 lost roughly a third of its value, and investors dumped stocks at a frantic pace.
While stock market crashes are not new, the speed of the market fall during the pandemic was unusual.
The initial recovery was also quick, as the S&P 500 had recovered to a new high by August 2020.
In the aftermath of the crash, many investors began to regret their decision to sell.
It is easy to avoid regret when the market is rising, but a market crash can leave many investors wondering what they did wrong.
Did they have too much of their portfolio in stocks?
Did they fail to keep up with the latest research?
The answer to both questions is usually no.
It is a rare investor who follows the latest research with perfect precision.
The market often performs well, and a successful investor likely did many things right.

When the market falls, it is easy to look back and start playing the game of “coulda, shoulda, woulda.” You could have had more in cash, you should have followed the latest research, you would have made more money.
Investors with a written plan, made in calm conditions, offer their future selves a rule to follow.
Investors who have decided in advance that they will not sell during a drawdown of less than X% give their future selves a rule to follow.
A well-crafted plan also gives your future self an answer to the question of how long the crisis will last.
The fact is that we will never know how long the crisis will last, but following a well-thought-out plan helps us make decisions even when we lack certainty.
The good news is that the market recovered quickly and the days of empty grocery shelves have passed, but these are lessons that should not be forgotten.
The next time we face a crisis, be it a pandemic, a market crash, or something else entirely, we will want to stock up and sell our stocks.
We will want to fill the gap with our best guess, and our best guess will be wrong.
The panic will lead us astray, and the crisis will feel intense, but we should keep our plans in mind.
A crisis is a challenging time for all of us, but remember that a crisis is also a time to learn.

There is a reason the most common phrase used by psychologists is “on average.” West and Stanovich found that having a system to identify our own flaws led to better decision making, and Kahneman later found that having a plan is a helpful tool in avoiding our own worst impulses.
Be prepared for the next crisis.
Think about how you will handle a crisis, and consider writing down a plan to help keep your future self on track.
It will take some effort, but it will pay off down the road.
- Keith Stanovich and Richard West, “Individual differences in reasoning: Implications for the rationality debate?
Ireland's Great Famine lasted from 1845 to 1852.
By the end, one million or more people had emigrated from the country, and Ireland's population fell by around a quarter.
When the trouble began, the weather had been cold and rainy, and many of the island's potatoes had rotted in the fields.
Then, in the autumn of 1845, farmers across Ireland found potatoes that looked healthy days earlier now rotting into black, foul-smelling slime.
The next year, the situation was worse.
By the time the blight had run its course in 1852, one million people or more had died of starvation or disease, and Ireland's population had fallen to 4.4 million from 4.15 million.
The Great Famine was the result of a funguslike organism, Phytophthora infestans, a water mold often called late blight.
The blight most likely arrived from the Americas in 1845, and it spread rapidly through Ireland's soggy, temperate fields.
Within three years, three-quarters of the island's croplands were infected.
The rot destroyed the country's staple food, a situation made worse when British landowners exported remaining crops to keep up with their payments.
The failure of the potato crop was also compounded by a failure of state relief efforts.
This story is a reminder that crops that look hearty and healthy today are much more fragile than they seem.
For much of the twentieth century, the world's export bananas were a single variety, Gros Michel.
It was tasty and it traveled well, so growers kept planting it — and clonal copies of it — in their plantations.
When a new strain of the fungus, Tropical Race 4, reared its head, it tore through the plantations in Central America, including in Costa Rica, forcing growers to abandon their fields.
Since then, the banana industry has switched to the resistant Cavendish variety, but it's not clear how long this will last.
The new strain of the fungus is on the march.
The Irish, the Gros Michel banana, and the Cavendish banana are all examples of a crop that loses its genetic diversity and becomes more susceptible to disease or pests.
The banana is a clonal crop, propagated by cuttings rather than seeds, but the pattern is the same for crops that are grown from seeds, too.
The Gros Michel banana was a disease-free, high-yielding variety, but it had a genetic weakness to the black sigatoka fungus.
Farmers compensated by spraying their crops with pesticides.
But now a new threat has emerged, and for which the Cavendish is as vulnerable as the Gros Michel was to black sigatoka.
A similar story played out in Ireland in the 1840.
Irish farmers grew predominantly one high-yielding variety, the "Lumper." But that variety lacked genetic resilience to the potato blight.
In the 1860, phylloxera, a tiny aphid-like insect that accidentally imported from North America, began devouring the roots of European grapevines.
The wine industry was saved by grafting European vines onto resistant American rootstocks, which drew on a different gene pool.
But the devastation was so severe that it took decades to rebuild the industry.
And the move away from clonal vines didn't happen for decades more.
Today, the lack of genetic diversity in European vineyards is again threatening the wine business.
In 1860, phylloxera destroyed a huge share of France's vineyards and devastated winemaking across Europe within a few decades.
If this sounds like the same pattern of narrowing a crop's genetic base, followed by something exploiting it sooner or later, that's because it is.
In 1970, the fungal disease southern corn leaf blight swept the United States, exploiting that shared trait.
It destroyed roughly 15 percent of the national corn crop, with losses far higher in some southern states.
The 1970 blight cost about a billion dollars.
Scientists think the southern corn leaf blight is caused by the same organism that led to the Irish potato famine: Phytophthora infestans, the water mold.
The fungus, which thrives in moist, humid weather, is still around.

In 1970, it lapped up a particular genetic trait that most American corn shared, "Texas male-sterile cytoplasm." It was a clever solution to a problem: how to get hybrid corn — which yields about 15 percent more than conventional corn — without spending time and resources on detasseling the crop.
The particular genetic trait made seed production cheaper, but it left the whole crop vulnerable to blight.
The southern corn leaf blight is just one example of the kind of damage that can be done to a crop with a narrow genetic base.
In 1845, the Irish potato famine was the result of that kind of vulnerability.
The Gros Michel banana collapse was also a result of a lack of genetic diversity.
Wheat rust, for example, has repeatedly ravaged crops thanks to a lack of genetic variation.
The Great Famine killed roughly one million people, and in the 1970, the blight was a big problem in the United States.
But in the 1970, the fungus destroyed crops across the world, leading to famines in several countries that killed an estimated five million people.
Today, a new strain, wheat stem rust race There is circulating in parts of the world.
And facilities like the Svalbard Global Seed Vault and national gene banks are safeguarding this genetic material.
The good news is that there's a lot of genetic variation out there.
Scientists are constantly searching the world for new traits that could help bolster our crops against disease and pests.
And biotech firms and academic labs are using cutting-edge breeding techniques to boost yields and find new crop varieties that can survive drought, heat, or colder temperatures.
The Food and Agriculture Policy is even working to improve the exchange of crop genetic material around the world.
The problem is that these crops don't always match up with what's being grown on the ground.
In many cases, a few high-yielding crop varieties have come to dominate the field.
In the 1960, the vast majority of the United States' hybrid corn carried the same genetic trait: "Texas male-sterile cytoplasm," which made seed production cheaper.
By the time the 1970 blight struck, the vast majority of corn in the United States shared the same genetic vulnerability.
And monocultures of high-yielding wheat strains have repeatedly led to widespread crop failures and famine.
All this is a reminder that crops that look hearty and healthy today are much more fragile than they seem.
In 1912, Congress passed the Aldrich-Vreeland Act, creating the National Monetary Commission to study banking reform.
Senator Nelson Aldrich, a Republican power broker whose daughter married John D.
Rockefeller Jr., was given the task of leading the commission.
In Aldrich's plan, a board of seven major financiers would manage a central bank that would expand and contract the currency in times of crisis to protect the interests of creditors.
But Wall Street had suffered a loss of confidence, and a major panic took hold in October 1907.
Depositors stormed banks across New York, and the treasury department was once again forced to bail out banks, including J.P.
Morgan, then seventy years old, summoned the city's leading bankers and trust company presidents to his private library on Madison Avenue.
"Gentle-men," he said, "you will have to support this bill or there will be war between the classes."
Morgan insisted that credit rested on "character" rather than money or property.
But his fellow bankers knew this was not so.
Credit rested on the assumption that if a bank made a loan and went bankrupt, a powerful uncle in the form of the Use Treasury would bail them out.
The Panic of 1907 had been stopped in its tracks when J.P.

Morgan, with the help of other major banks, rescued his own bank and the stock market by cornering the market on stocks, forcing the stock price higher, and loaning tens of millions to his bank and his friends.
By some accounts Morgan had locked the doors until the bankers agreed to pool funds and stop the run.

But everyone knew that the real rescue had been the decision of Secretary of the Treasury, (and future president) Wilson, to "suspend specie payment," meaning that the Treasury would sit out the storm and continue to make loans.
Wilson was no fan of Wall Street.
He had been quoted in the newspapers saying: "The great monopoly in this country is the money monopoly.
So long as that exists, our old variety of freedom will never be restored, no matter what laws are enacted."
While the two sides argued, the American public was still uneasy.

Anxious for reform, Democrats swept the 1912 elections and reformed the central banking act once again, this time calling it the Federal Reserve Act, which was steered by Representative Carter Glass, a former newspaper editor who had once written that "Money is a creature of law and the original issue of money must be by an act of legislation." The Aldrich Plan would not fly.
Democrats wanted a decentralized system, and one that would be under the direct control of the public, not bankers.

By some accounts the final plan for the Federal Reserve System was hatched on November 22, 1910, when Senator Aldrich met with five of the country's most powerful bankers at the private resort island off the coast of Georgia called Jekyll Island, where they spent roughly ten days drafting the blueprint for what became the Federal Reserve System.
The men were honking geese, barking dogs, and horse-drawn carriages as they came one at a time, using only first names, to what they told the public was a duck-hunting trip.
The men drafted what would become known as the Federal Reserve Act.
The secrecy was so tight that the names of the participants were not revealed until 1935, when the New York Federal Reserve branch held a dedication of a plaque in honor of the event.

One of the participants, Frank Vanderlip, then president of National City Bank, a Rockefeller-aligned bank, would later write: "I was as secretive—indeed, as furtive—as any conspirator" in a 1935 Saturday Evening Post article.
Vanderlip said that if the meeting had been exposed, "it would have been fatally embarrassing to Wall Street." Indeed it would have.
The list of participants at the Jekyll Island meeting included Henry P.
Morgan & Co.; Paul Warburg, partner at Kuhn, Loeb & Co.; Senator Aldrich; A.
Piatt Andrew, assistant secretary of the Treasury; and Charles D.
Norton, president of the Morgan-affiliated First National Bank of New York.
As partners and officers at J.P.

Their holdings represented a whopping $22 billion of resources, nearly half of the nation's total corporate resources.
By 1912 the banks whose officials had gathered at Jekyll Island held 341 percent of all deposits in the country and 23 percent of all bank assets.

A separate commission, headed by the economist Paul Warburg, the son of one of the founders of Kuhn, Loeb & Co.

I was heartbroken to hear my 10-year-old grandson use Jesus' name as a casual expletive the other day.
I call it the "high school" or "locker room" level of blasphemy, not quite as bad as some of the other slang terms for God, but still very sad.
It is such a mark of spiritual immaturity.
Of course, Jesus' name is used as a casual expletive by many people, including Christians, but I would like to get us away from that practice and instead see Jesus for who He really is.
I want to know the historical Jesus, the one who lived in first-century Palestine, who taught crowds, who healed the sick, and who was executed under Pontius Pilate.
But I also want to know the Jesus of the New Testament, the Jesus who claimed to be the way, the truth, and the life, and who by the testimony of his followers rose from the dead.

While I think we can learn much about who Jesus is by reading one of the Gospels, perhaps the shortest and most direct, Mark, I would also suggest that we learn much about who Jesus is by getting to know Saul of Tarsus.
Saul didn't know the historical Jesus but he knew the Jesus of the New Testament.
Saul was brilliant, devout, and zealous, trained in the Jewish law.
He went from house to house, dragging believers off to prison, and he believed the growing movement of Jesus' followers was a dangerous heresy, and so set out to destroy it.
But on a road to Damascus something like scales fell from Saul's eyes and he could see again.
A voice said "Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me?" And when Saul asked "Who are you, Lord?" the answer was, "I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting."

Saul was blinded for three days and then a follower of Jesus, an Ananias, afraid but obedient, went to Saul, laid hands on him, and called him "brother." Saul was baptized, he began to proclaim that Jesus is the Son of God, and he was imprisoned, beaten, and on more than one occasion almost killed.
At the same time he planted churches across the Roman world, he endured beatings, shipwrecks, and imprisonment, and wrote much of the New Testament.
He is known today as Paul, the apostle to the gentiles, a man who gave his life to Jesus.
I don't know what the historical Jesus was like.
Did He have a warm smile or a mysterious glance?
But I do know the Jesus of the New Testament and I want you to know him, too.
I want you to know Jesus as Paul knew him, the Jesus who changed his life and changed the course of history.

In his letter to the Philippians, Paul wrote that "at the name of Jesus every knee should bow" and that "every tongue confess that Jesus Christ is Lord." That Jesus, the Jesus of the New Testament, is the one we worship, the one we sing to, the one we give our lives to.
It's the one who brings meaning to our world and hope to our future.
It's the one who heals our hearts and who fills our lives with joy.
It's the one who died on a cross and rose from the dead, it's the one who calls us to repentance, who promises to transform our lives, who promises to make all things new.
It's the one who is worthy of our worship and our devotion.
Saul of Tarsus knew that Jesus.
